explanations.answer: In the greatness of His strength
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text asks, "Who is this robed in splendor, marching in the greatness of His strength?" (Isaiah 63:1). Splendor on the outside, strength in every step. I couldn't march like that if you gave me a tailwind and a gold base with wheels.

explanations.answer: In the weariness of a long road
explanations.explanation: I get the guess, friend. Coming all the way from Edom sounds like it would wear a person out. But the text never says He's weary. It says He is "…marching in the greatness of His strength?" (Isaiah 63:1). This One is not dragging His feet.

explanations.answer: In the sorrow of a heavy heart
explanations.explanation: Stained garments can make a scene feel sad, so I see why you picked it. But the verse doesn't say anything about sorrow in His march. It says He is "…robed in splendor, marching in the greatness of His strength?" (Isaiah 63:1). Strength is the word, friend.
True, baker! He answers the question Himself: "It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save." (Isaiah 63:1). He doesn't give a name here. He tells you what He does.

Not quite, friend. The One from Edom answers the question about who He is, and He says, "It is I, proclaiming vindication, mighty to save." (Isaiah 63:1). So He does say it, in His own words. Easy one to second-guess, though.

Yes, baker. The question asks, "Why are Your clothes red, and Your garments like one who treads the winepress?" (Isaiah 63:2). A winepress is where people trod on grapes to squeeze out the juice. Anybody who's done that comes out stained, and I'd be the same way after a dive into the chocolate chips.

Good thinking, friend. A threshing floor is a place of hard work, but this verse is about something else. The garments are "…like one who treads the winepress?" (Isaiah 63:2). So the answer is the winepress.
I see why fire came to mind with all that red. But the text doesn't mention an altar here. It says His garments are "…like one who treads the winepress?" (Isaiah 63:2). Wine, not smoke, friend.
That's it, baker. He says, "For the day of vengeance was in My heart…" (Isaiah 63:4). It's a heavy word, and the text doesn't soften it. So we don't either.
Rest is a lovely word, friend, and I'd take a nap right now. But that isn't what's in His heart here. The verse says, "For the day of vengeance was in My heart…" (Isaiah 63:4).
Mourning fits a sad scene, so I understand the pick. But the verse uses a different word: "For the day of vengeance was in My heart…" (Isaiah 63:4). Vengeance is the one that belongs in that blank.

Close, friend, but that's not what the verse says. He says, "For the day of vengeance was in My heart, and the year of My redemption had come." (Isaiah 63:4). Had come, not far off. The two are named side by side.
Right, baker! The verse says, "…and the year of My redemption had come." (Isaiah 63:4). It's not far off at all. It had come, and it sits right next to the day of vengeance.
I can see why you'd wonder, friend. But the text never says relief. He says, "I was appalled that no one assisted." (Isaiah 63:5). Appalled is the opposite of relieved.
Yes, baker. No relief here. He says, "I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled that no one assisted." (Isaiah 63:5). Appalled, plain and simple.
That's right, baker. He says, "I looked, but there was no one to help…" and then, "So My arm brought Me salvation…" (Isaiah 63:5). No one helped Him. His own arm did the work.

Good guess on who might show up, but the nations are on the other side of this scene. He says, "…no one from the nations was with Me." (Isaiah 63:3). What brought salvation? "…My arm brought Me salvation…" (Isaiah 63:5).
An army would be a reasonable thing to expect, friend. But the text mentions no army. He says, "I looked, but there was no one to help…" and then, "So My arm brought Me salvation…" (Isaiah 63:5).
